title: How ACGME-Compliant Call Schedules Actually Get Built
description: How the ACGME work hour rules play out in surgery and IM call schedules, why flagging violations afterwards is not enough, and what building them in looks like.
content:
Summary

  • The ACGME duty hour rules interlock, and specialties add their own on top, which makes call schedules easy to get wrong by hand.
  • When the rules are only checked after the schedule is built, the chief resident is left fixing problems and re-checking.
  • The alternative is to write the rules down first and build the schedule to them, so the review at the end is a check, not a repair job.
  • Managed services like Scheduling Wizard deliver finished schedules built to the rules, removing the operator burden and providing continuity year after year.

Every chief resident knows the feeling: it's late, you've got a half-finished call schedule open in a spreadsheet, and you're not entirely sure if what you've built meets ACGME compliance rules.

You've mentally run through the 80-hour rule, tried to account for the rest period requirements (eight hours off between scheduled work periods), and made sure no one is on call more than every third night, but there's always that nagging doubt. Did the rules change again? Are you applying them correctly for your specialty?

That doubt is reasonable. The common duty hour rules have been stable since 2017, but specialties add their own requirements, and programs read the gray areas differently. The ACGME Program Requirements make clear that the common framework is just a floor, so specialties layer their own requirements on top, and the permutations multiply fast. For a program building call by hand, that variation is where compliance problems come from.

The ACGME Work Hour Rules a Call Schedule Has to Meet

Most people in Graduate Medical Education (GME) know the headline rule: residents cannot exceed 80 hours per week, averaged over four weeks. But that's barely scratching the surface. A published review of residency scheduling highlights the full web of interlocking rules that any compliant schedule must satisfy simultaneously:

  • 80-hour weekly limit: averaged over 4 weeks, inclusive of all in-house work, clinical work from home and moonlighting
  • One day off in seven: averaged over 4 weeks, a full 24-hour period free from clinical duties
  • Call frequency cap: in-house call no more than every third night (Q3 call), averaged over 4 weeks
  • Continuous duty limit: the 24+4 rule (24 consecutive hours of scheduled clinical work, with up to 4 additional hours for transitions of care and/or education). This rule applies to all residents. PGY-1 residents were capped at 16 hours until 2017.
  • Rest period: eight hours off between scheduled periods (worded as a should), and at least 14 hours free after 24 hours of in-house call
  • At-home call: time spent on clinical work from home or returning to the hospital counts toward the 80-hour limit, averaged over four weeks

The 24+4 rule has applied at every level since 2017: PGY-1 residents, who were capped at 16 hours before that, may be scheduled for 24-hour shifts with the four-hour transition allowance. A program that still builds intern rotations around a 16-hour cap is not wrong, just stricter than the rule requires. And these rules don't apply uniformly across specialties. That's where scheduling gets hard.

A Tale of Two Specialties: Surgery vs. Internal Medicine

To understand why subspecialty-specific rules matter, consider how differently a general surgery call schedule and an internal medicine call schedule need to be built, even though both programs operate under the same ACGME umbrella.

General Surgery

Surgery programs operate under intense scrutiny around consecutive duty hours. The 24-hour cap on scheduled work bites hardest here. The temptation to keep a post-call resident for one more elective case is where the four-hour transition window most often gets stretched.

Off-duty minimums between shifts must be built into the schedule proactively, not just checked retroactively. Moonlighting counts: any moonlighting hours, internal or external, count toward the 80-hour cap (averaged over four weeks), and must be logged, something that is easy to lose track of because it requires active tracking across the schedule.

Internal Medicine

IM programs have a different scheduling profile. The continuity-of-care model means scheduling logic often centers on cumulative hour loads distributed across weeks, not just day-to-day shift boundaries. Continuity clinic the morning after call is a common collision in IM.

Home call is common in IM, and residents are often unsure whether their at-home call response time and frequency is being correctly counted toward their weekly hours. Moonlighting restrictions also differ: some IM programs permit external moonlighting for PGY-2s and above with specific documentation, while others do not, and PGY-1s may not moonlight at all under the Common Program Requirements.

So a call template that works for an IM program will not necessarily carry over to surgery, and whoever builds the schedule has to know which rules apply where.

Why Checking the Call Schedule Afterwards Is Not Enough

When chief residents go looking for help, they often land on one of two options: build the schedule manually in Excel, or adopt a self-service scheduling tool. Either way, the person doing the build carries the rules, and checking often happens at the end.

As residents and program coordinators have noted in online discussions, even AI-assisted tools "often require a lot of manual scheduling." The user still bears the compliance burden.

The software surfaces violations after the fact, and someone (usually the chief resident) has to manually resolve them.

Three things make this hard for a chief resident:

  1. Checking comes last. Finding a broken rule after the build is useful, but it leaves the fix to the chief.
  2. Someone has to run it. With self-service software the chief resident learns the platform, sets up the ACGME rules for their specialty, enters every resident's requests and works the output into shape. Building these schedules often takes 10 to 15 hours per cycle, time that a chief resident simply shouldn't have to spend.
  3. Institutional knowledge walks out the door every year. The current chief knows which residents have specific rules, which rotations have coverage gaps, and how the schedule bends under pressure. When the chief rotates out, that knowledge disappears. The next chief starts from scratch, often making the same mistakes and exposing the program to the same compliance risks.

From Checking Afterwards to Building It In

The other approach is to have a team build the schedule to the rules from the start, rather than building it and checking it afterwards.

In practice that means every rule, the ACGME ones and the program's own, is written down before the first assignment is made, and the schedule is built to all of them at once. The review at the end is then a check, not a repair job.

That approach is the foundation of a managed scheduling service. Instead of leaving the work to the chief resident, these services deliver a finished schedule. Scheduling Wizard is one such service. Programs send their rules and receive the finished call, block, clinic and attending schedules, built to the ACGME requirements they tell us apply, delivered as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for them.

In practice:

  • The rules go in first. The team writes down the subspecialty-specific ACGME rules you tell us apply, including duty hour limits, consecutive hour caps, rest period minimums, moonlighting restrictions, and call frequency rules, and builds the schedule so they hold.
  • The operator burden goes away. Chief residents don't need to learn scheduling software or spend 10-15 hours per cycle in a spreadsheet. They submit rules; they receive a finished schedule.
  • Institutional knowledge persists. Because Scheduling Wizard keeps the written rules for each program, the rule set doesn't evaporate when the chief resident rotates. Programs retain continuity across annual leadership transitions.
  • It works alongside the tools programs already use. You can upload the finished schedule into the platform you already use, use our live view, or both; it is entirely up to you.

Build It In, Then Review Once

The ACGME duty hour rules are a lot to hold in your head while building a call schedule. Subspecialty-specific requirements, the 24+4 rule, moonlighting accounting, at-home call tracking, and the interlocking nature of all these rules together create a surface area for error that grows with every scheduling cycle.

So the choice for chief residents and program directors is about approach as much as tools. Checking after the fact leaves the fixing with the program. A team that builds the rules in from the first assignment removes most of that exposure.

Build the schedule with the rules in it, then review it once rather than repairing it over and over.

Frequently Asked Questions

How does Scheduling Wizard handle the ACGME rules for my specific subspecialty?

You tell us which requirements apply to your program, the Common Program Requirements and anything your specialty's Review Committee adds, and we write them down with you alongside your own rules before the first build. They go into the schedule while it is built rather than being flagged afterwards. We do not assume we know your requirements better than you do; we ask.

Do we have to change the platform we already use?

No. It is entirely up to you. We build the schedule either way, and deliver it in the format and structure you want: Excel or Google Sheets, or a custom live view we build for you if that is useful. Many programs keep the platform they already have for day-to-day viewing and upload our schedules straight into it; others use the live view, or both. Whatever works best for your program.

What are the current ACGME duty hour rules?

80 hours a week averaged over four weeks, with clinical work from home, at-home call activity and moonlighting all counted; no more than 24 hours of continuous scheduled work plus up to four for transitions, at every PGY level; at least 14 hours free after 24 hours of in-house call; one day in seven free, averaged over four weeks, with no at-home call on it; and in-house call no more often than every third night. These have been in place since the 2017 revision.

How is Scheduling Wizard different from self-service scheduling software?

Scheduling Wizard is a managed "done-for-you" service, not self-service software, which means the operator burden goes away. With traditional software, the chief resident or coordinator must learn the platform, input all rules, and manually fix any errors. With Scheduling Wizard, you simply submit your requirements, and our team delivers the finished schedule, built to the rules. We do the building, so you don't have to.

Can individual resident requests and preferences be part of the build?

Yes, we incorporate a wide range of individual requests, fairness rules, and complex preferences alongside ACGME rules. We build around specific vacation requests, day-off preferences, and fairness rules (e.g., providing an even distribution of weekend calls). These are treated as requests we work to satisfy while holding the ACGME requirements and clinical coverage fixed.

What is the process for getting a schedule from Scheduling Wizard?

The process is simple: you provide us with your program's specific rules, and we deliver a finished schedule built to your rules as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you. Our process involves an initial consultation to write down your program's rules. For each scheduling cycle, you'll submit any updates and resident requests, and our team builds the schedule for you.

Who typically uses Scheduling Wizard? Is it just for residents?

Scheduling Wizard is used by chief residents, program directors, and coordinators in GME programs, as well as by administrators in private physician practices. Most of our work is residency and fellowship scheduling under the ACGME requirements, and we also build attending, hospitalist and private practice call schedules.

If you would rather hand the build over, book a call and tell us how your call schedules work. We build to your rules and requests, with the ACGME requirements as part of them, and send back the finished schedule.
